context_blurb:
Look at a tree, a lawn or a pot of basil on a windowsill. Not one of them ever eats. Green plants make their own food instead, right in their leaves, with the help of sunlight. The energy in your lunch began this way too, caught from the Sun by a plant.

A plant's way of making its own food from water and air, powered by sunlight, is called photosynthesis. The word comes from Greek: photo means light, and synthesis means putting together, so photosynthesis is putting together with light. A photograph is named for the same Greek word, because it is a drawing made with light.

A plant needs three things to make its food. Sunlight gives the energy. Water comes up through the roots. From the air, the plant takes in carbon dioxide, a gas that makes up only a tiny part of the air. Plants take in some oxygen too, but they use it to break their food down for energy, not to make it. Inside the leaf, the plant uses the light's energy to build sugar out of the water and carbon dioxide, and that sugar is its food. The sugar feeds every part of the plant, and any spare is stored as starch, a plant's packed-away food.

Leaves are the plant's food factories, because a plant can make food only where light reaches its green parts. Think of a potato plant. The potatoes sit underground, stuffed with food, but they did not make it, for no light reaches them down in the dark soil, and none reaches the roots either. The leaves above ground make sugar in the sunlight, and it travels down the plant to the potatoes, where it is stored as starch.

You can watch a plant making food. Set a sprig of pondweed in a jar of water in bright sunshine, and tiny bubbles soon gather on its leaves and drift upward. As the pondweed makes its food, its leaves give off oxygen, and the oxygen rises in the bubbles. Carry the jar into the dark, and the bubbles soon stop. The oxygen that plants give off is the same oxygen people and animals breathe.

Now for the biggest surprise. A little acorn can become an enormous oak, so where does all that wood come from? Many people guess the soil, but the soil gives a tree only small amounts of minerals. A tree builds its wood mostly out of air and water: carbon dioxide from the air, and water from the ground. Sunlight supplies the energy for the building, but none of the stuff itself. About four hundred years ago, Jan Baptist van Helmont planted a small willow in a pot holding 200 pounds of dried soil and gave it nothing but water for five years. The willow gained over 160 pounds, yet the soil lost only about two ounces. He thought the water had built it all, and never guessed how much came from the air.

The Sun's energy does not stop at the plant. As grass makes its food, it catches energy from sunlight and stores that energy in its sugar. A cow grazing in a field takes that energy in, and it lets her move about and stay warm. The soil, the rain and the air give the grass things to build with, but no energy at all. So the cow runs on energy that was once the Sun's light, and so do you.
